Our job was to close July for Kalmora, a group of seven companies. We get raw material: 305 supplier documents, 48 bank statements in three formats, and an ERP export with over a hundred thousand journal lines. We have to hand in six files, and a grader checks them line by line. So this is really a data pipeline. I'll walk you through it in four steps.

Step one is reading the files. PDFs with a text layer go through pypdf. XML invoices, Spanish Facturae and Mexican CFDI, we parse as structured data. When a PDF comes with them we compare the two, and if the number or the amounts differ, we flag it. Scanned PDFs have no text, so we run Apple's Vision OCR on the Mac. Nothing leaves the machine. Bank statements come as N43, camt.053 and CSV. We parse the originals because they carry references the ERP export drops, like the mandate or the invoice number. Everything is cached by file hash and parser version, so a re-run doesn't read anything twice.

event_key is unique. The same event can't be booked twice.

Step two: everything goes into one SQLite file. Each ERP export becomes a table. The journal alone is about 110 thousand lines, and the extracted documents and bank lines sit next to it. Then six tasks run in a fixed order: payables, billing, bank, intercompany, cash and close. Each one reads a view called ledger, which is what's already posted plus what earlier tasks have proposed, and writes its own entries back. Every entry has an event key, and that key is unique. If two tasks try to book the same event, the database refuses. That's how we avoid double posting without coordinating by hand.

The account comes from the vendor's history. Journal text is truncated, so we match the first 12 characters.

12 entries fixed
Step three is cleaning. There are a lot of rules; here are four. One: the same invoice arrives twice, once as F-dash-26012023 and once as 26012023. We normalize the number the way the grader does, so the second one is marked duplicate and never booked. Two: an invoice addressed to company 1910, but the direct debit came out of company 1100's account. We check the mandate against the bank master and reject it as wrong addressee. Three: Mexican invoices come as XML and PDF. The XML has no guarantee retention, the PDF does. Our merge used to drop it. Now it keeps it, and five entries got fixed. Four: invoices without a purchase order. Which expense account? We look at what the same vendor was booked to for the same concept before. The journal text is cut short, so we match on the first twelve characters. Twelve entries improved.

Step four: decide. Rules come first and they decide almost everything. When no rule can, we send the evidence to Claude with the accounting policies and a closed list of options. We only accept the answer if it's one of those options and the confidence is at least 0.8, and we cache it so runs repeat exactly. Otherwise we take the safe option, which is not posting, and write the case to a doubts file for a person. Every entry also goes through a validator: whole cents, debit or credit, and it has to balance per company. And here's why the shared ledger matters. A customer owes 438 thousand. The bank receives 430. The gap is the agent's fee. Payables books the fee, the bank task explains the deposit, and cash application nets the two. Nothing is left open.

182 automated tests. Next: accruals in close. The test set has no answer key, so its score is unknown.

Billing, cash, bank and intercompany are at 1.0: every item, every receipt, all twelve bank accounts, all five intercompany differences. The trial balance is off by 0.06 percent. Two bars are lower. Payables at 0.969, and if we break it down by decision, HOLD is where we lose: invoices we stopped that the answer key posts, or the other way round. And close at 0.856, which is accruals. That's where the next day would go. The test set has no answer key, so we don't know that score yet. Thanks.
